input.title: The loop's highlights never reach me unless I go digging
input.parent: Checking on progress means digging through files
input.body:
**The need (founder's voice, 2026-08-11, verbatim in substance):** "If a red test goes green, I'm not notified. If a long-standing opportunity gets killed, I'm not made aware of the reasons... I'd like to be at least notified of the highlights, but I haven't found a good way to helping you determine what's worth sharing, nor am I certain that the highlights are happening as hoped." And the success criterion behind it: "I want this whole build + discover loop to be a compute success, not my success... the thesis gets proven if it can succeed on its own."

**What the record shows against it (observed counts from the same session):** 20 post-build red-to-green observations and 4 was-already-green records sit in vault history and none was ever surfaced as a highlight. Per-firing reports exist but carry one paragraph per firing, not milestones. No opportunity has ever been killed, because kill/promote is human-only today — so half the highlight classes the founder wants notification for are events the current doctrine cannot produce without him, a boundary any solution here must respect rather than quietly relax.

**The trust cost, observed the same night:** the build loop reported "NOT MERGED" on PRs #94 and #95 while GitHub showed both merged in the same minute, and eight PRs (#88–#95) sat merged while the founder said "I don't get much reassurance that the build loop is building anything." A false failure report is the inverse of a highlight, and it burned exactly the trust that surfaced highlights would have built.

**Litmus — more than one way to address this:** yes. Announce each transition the moment it is observed; distill a per-firing or periodic digest from what history already records; let the founder curate what counts as a highlight in a durable artifact the loop reads; keep a milestone ledger a human reads at their own cadence. Passes.

**Distinctness.** The parent category holds the pull-side pain — finding out anything means digging through files. This node is the push side: the milestones themselves should announce their occurrence. It is also distinct from "A block stops everything and announces itself to no one", which is about waits and blocks; this is about wins and verdicts.

**Provenance caveat:** founder first-person account (stated), with observed counts recorded beside it in the source note. The counts say highlights exist unsurfaced; only the founder can say which of them he would have wanted.

input.title: Announce a red-to-green flip on the founder's channel the moment it is observed
input.parent: The loop's highlights never reach me unless I go digging
input.body:
When a post-build observation records an instrument going from red to green, send one short push message to a channel the founder already watches, at the moment the flip is recorded — the event, the solution it clears, and where the observation lives.

**Against the alternatives beside it:** this is the immediate, event-granular end of the spectrum. It needs no curation artifact and no digest cadence, and it surfaces the win while the context is fresh. Its risk is the known one recorded for block notifications — interrupts that arrive too often stop being read — and red-to-green flips are rarer than blocks, which is the reason to believe the risk is smaller here. It cannot surface opportunity-kill highlights, because those events do not occur without a human today.

input.title: A highlights digest distilled from what vault history already records
input.parent: The loop's highlights never reach me unless I go digging
input.body:
A periodic (per-firing or daily) digest that reads what the vault already records — the 20 unsurfaced red-to-green observations existed in history the night the founder said he heard nothing — ranks the entries, and delivers a short highlights message. Nothing new is measured; the gap this closes is that recorded milestones are written where nobody reads.

**Against the alternatives beside it:** batched rather than interruptive, so it trades immediacy for signal density and is harder to tune out. It depends on one belief the flip-announcement does not: that what the founder means by "highlights" is already present in recorded history rather than being a kind of event nothing records yet — his own caveat ("nor am I certain that the highlights are happening as hoped") says he does not know either, which is exactly what a sample digest would settle.

input.title: A highlight criteria note the founder edits and the loop reads before deciding what to surface
input.parent: The loop's highlights never reach me unless I go digging
input.body:
A small durable note in the vault — "what counts as a highlight" — that the founder edits in his own words and every reporting surface consults before deciding what to push. Seeded with the two classes he already named (a red test going green; a long-standing branch dying, with reasons), and grown by him as surfaced non-highlights teach him what he did not mean.

**Against the alternatives beside it:** this attacks the blocker the founder actually stated — "I haven't found a good way to helping you determine what's worth sharing" — by making the sharing criteria a durable, editable artifact instead of a judgement re-guessed every firing. It is the only candidate that improves the other two rather than competing with them (both flip announcements and digests would read it). Its own risk is viability: a criteria note only works if the founder actually maintains it, and every prior artifact that asked for recurring founder input is evidence to check that belief against.

input.title: Highlight interrupts keep their signal — the founder keeps reading them rather than tuning them out
input.parent: Announce a red-to-green flip on the founder's channel the moment it is observed
input.body: Desirability. The belief: red-to-green flip announcements arrive rarely enough, and matter enough, that the founder keeps reading and reacting to them instead of muting the channel. Stated so it could be false: the founder could tune them out within a week, the way the tree already suspects operators tune out block notifications ("An operator notified at every block keeps acting on the notifications rather than tuning them out" records the same worry for a different event class). If false, the immediate-announcement solution delivers noise, not reassurance, and the digest or criteria-note alternatives should win the comparison.

input.title: Send flip announcements for two weeks and count which ones the founder reacts to
input.parent: Highlight interrupts keep their signal — the founder keeps reading them rather than tuning them out
input.humansRequired: The founder's own attention is the measurement — only he can read, ignore, or mute the announcements, and only his reactions say whether the signal survived.
input.threshold: At least 3 of the first 5 announcements draw a founder reaction (reply, follow-up, or named in conversation) within a day of arriving; zero reactions to the last 5 of the trial counts as tuned out.
input.body: Small and fast: for two weeks, whenever a post-build observation records a red-to-green flip, a human relays one short announcement to the channel the founder already watches — no build needed, a manual relay is the test. Count reactions. This probes only the tuning-out belief; it says nothing about whether flips are the highlights the founder most wants (the digest test beside this probes content), and a two-week founder-of-one sample generalizes to nobody else.

input.title: Hand the founder a digest built from last month's history and ask what it missed
input.parent: What the founder means by highlights is already present in vault history
input.humansRequired: Only the founder can say whether the highlights he wanted are in the digest — the question is what he meant, and no repository or spec can answer for him.
input.threshold: The founder names at most 2 highlight classes the digest missed, and names at least 1 entry he would not otherwise have known about. Three or more named misses falsifies the belief that history already holds what he means.
input.body: Small and fast: an attended session compiles one digest by hand from the last month of vault history (the 20 recorded red-to-green observations and 4 was-already-green records are the known raw material), hands it to the founder, and asks two questions — what here would you have wanted pushed to you, and what happened last month that this misses? No code is built; the digest is compiled once, manually. This is comparative evidence for choosing between digest and criteria-note: every missed class the founder names is a criteria-note entry the history does not yet record.
